What does it take to start and scale a successful business today?

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Sonia Zebadua and Alexandra Osan from Multiservices Vancouver to find out. Between them, they've spent more than a decade building and running multiple successful businesses.

13 years ago, Sonia started a cleaning company where she was the only employee. Today she, Alex and Michelle Rustrian Lopez run MSV, a commercial and construction cleaning company. Along the way, they also opened eight Mi Tierra Latina Stores.

I asked them a few quick-fire questions on how they'd start and scale a business today:
Start alone or with a business partner? "Partner."
Google Ads? "Used to, not anymore."
One service or many? "Multiple."
More leads, or follow up on the ones you have? "Following up on leads you have."
Biggest mistake new owners make? "Thinking you can do everything yourself." And: "Try to please everybody."

And a bonus one for Alex: what's your favourite thing you've automated with Barry?
"A morning message. Not even my partner does that." 🫣

MSV runs more than 20 WhatsApp group chats for just one of their businesses, with crews reporting in at 3 or 4 in the morning. Now, with Barry, Alex wakes up to one message with the jobs coming up and the issues reported overnight. She says it gives her back up to 10 hours a week.

Thanks, Alex and Sonia, for being great sports. Watch the full round below.

I found $700,000 in service revenue by accident.

I was digging through 1,300 of Mae - Making Auto Easy's service advisor transcripts with customers, hunting for CSI risks to warn Service Managers (yes, Mae is in the service drive now too!). Which we found many, of course.

Then I found something else: money nobody was chasing. 

Nobody dropped the ball. Every advisor did their job. Every customer got taken care of.

But buried in all that small talk, day-in-day-out, were customers hinting at what they wanted next. 

💬 "My daughter thinks we need a smaller SUV."

💬  "I'll do the repair, maybe next time."

In fact, 27% of service conversations left work on the table. And best part is, 60% of those customers already said YES to coming back!! 

But then... No appointment. No follow-up. No call.

So where's the system that's supposed to catch that?

Here's the real problem: we're asking one person to hear everything, remember everything, and follow up on everything — while the next customer is already pulling in. 🤯🤯  

That's not a training problem. That's a memory problem.

So that's what Mae is for. Not replacing the conversation. Just making sure it doesn't disappear the second it's over.

We threw out our AI product and started over. Best decision ever.

Here's what happened. We kept hearing that people liked what we built, but the usage numbers were telling us a different story. So instead of guessing, we sat back down with the problem and talked to our customers to find the root problems, again. 🫠 

The lesson hit fast. Our desktop solution was getting confusing and it didn't fit every dealership's sales process. We needed something that could keep pace with the floor, not slow it down. Our product wasn't meeting them where they are.

So we rebuilt the whole thing as a mobile app. Integrated right into the CRM systems they already use. Everything one to three clicks away for the salespeople to make their lives easier. 

The numbers backed it up. Adoption climbed. Utilization climbed. And we quadrupled the data and the recorded session time dealerships are capturing.
Turns out the fastest way to build the right thing is to stop building and go listen!

Eric Denlinger
Back in 2021 they invested in who grew the fastest, but today it’s not just about growth potential. He’s looking at strong unit economics, profitability and retention. Are we capturing the right ICP, the ones that stay?

David Metter

Daniel Raglan
When judging deals, it’s about sentiment, data and AI.

Jason Scott
Metal is the smallest part of the car business. The real value is LTV of the relationship and the data.

Ryan Maher
Workflow management is going away. Stop making people click the buttons to get the workflows. Focus on the solution that gives you just the outcomes. I am 1000% with you on this Ryan.

Ron Frey
When we think about defensibility and partnering with large companies, really consider about how adding our integration into their process and deep expertise helps to build defensibility.

When large companies think about acquiring smaller ones, they are evaluating energy and risk. What are they trying to accomplish? How can we make that easier for them?

“What do you hate?”
a.k.a. my new favorite question to ask users.
Because asking what they wanted wasn't working this time.

I spent a couple days with my users (dealership salespeople) and asking what they wanted in the next big feature we were designing.

Aka: “If I build this, will you actually use it?”

I was obviously fighting for validation - a clear answer that I was building the right thing.

But instead, I ended up spinning in circles because:
1️⃣ People don’t always know what they want, and sometimes they aren't seeing what’s possible.
2️⃣ Too many ideas means chasing scope creep trying to build it all.
3️⃣ And worst of all, you collect so much feedback that you lose the signal.

The truth? There is no one big reveal.

So instead, I’m learning to:
• Take the signals
• Break them down into an MVP
• Test behavior
• Trust the vision ✨

A dealership VP asked me: “Do you have any basic tips to help our team start adopting AI and actually be more productive?”

It got me thinking so I came up with a whole list of:
 1️⃣ Productivity tips for General Managers
 2️⃣ Hacks GMs can teach to their teams

But here are the 3 that helped me accelerate my own adoption and different aha moments:

1. Create your dream board of advisors 🔮 
I built a custom GPT where Steve Jobs and Mary Barra “duke it out” on big topics in the same room. Steve pushes to think 10x and be a visionary, and Mary counters and grounds us in the reality of how auto works.

2. Sales pitch feedback and role-play to a Dealership persona I created 🤼 
It throws common and tough objections at me from the perspective of a GM or SM, then shares feedback to my response. Or I'll upload transcripts from my sales pitches to find tendencies and ways to improve (for example: I’m very transparent, but I need to watch that I don’t over-explain or apologize) 😅 

3. Speak, don't type w/ voice AI 🎤 
I speak at 150+ words per minute, but typing slows me down by having to  think about typing the right sentence. Dictating my thoughts to ChatGPT lets me think out loud and move waaay faster.

For example, several dealers I’ve talked to recently are revamping their onboarding process right now. Instead of typing it out, ask ChatGPT to generate 10 questions about onboarding — then just talk your way through the answers (even better, have your team in the room too) and let AI get you the best first draft.

Which made me realize this about adoption:
Using AI is just step 1 ✨
Step 2 is becoming AI-literate 🪄

“There is no comfort in growth, and no growth in comfort.”
Kathy Gilbert said this at Day 1 at Women In Automotive. 

It's the quote that hit me the hardest. 
It's so simple, and yet so easy to forget. 

Building a startup means doing something that feels risky every day. 
Every time I’ve felt scared, uncertain, or out of my depth - those are actually the moments that count the most. 

Putting my corporate career to the side.
Forgoing an easy six-figure salary for another year.
Wanting to quit when things aren’t working or moving too slowly.
Standing in a crowd of experts and wondering if I belong.

Now I just remind myself that in this moment, I am growing.
And that this moment counts.

And the discomfort?
Maybe that's exactly where I belong.

Here's to the next best year of my life 🚀

I fired my first customer and I’d do it again.

Their leader had quit. They said they needed to cut costs.
I did what anyone in sales would do: listen, ask questions, find opportunities, offer discounts.

So I saved the deal! 

But the truth is, without someone at the helm who knows what they want and to champion your product, building cool one-off features to keep things alive is the ultimate distraction.

It was a hard decision, but obviously the right one.

Figuring out who my Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) is NOT is just as important as knowing who IS. 

Letting them go means I could double down with dealerships who are ready and believes in our vision.

Now I know who I want to work with:
- Dealership GMs that are hungry and can name their pain
- High sales team turnover 
- Still using manual systems like the paper guest sheet
- Sales teams that are younger, not the “usual car person”
- CRM utilization they’re not happy with

That’s my ICP. That’s who I’m building for.
Or I guess you could say, my IDP (Ideal Dealership Profile) 🤓

I shared my story, my process, and the frameworks that led Mae - Making Auto Easy from something that “kinda works” into “holy shit we just closed our first enterprise deal”.

The talk itself? It flew by.

Had an incredible evening getting to know the other BCBusiness 30 Under 30 winners last night 🍻 

Emails and LinkedIn messages are great for quick questions, but I'm still a strong believer that the best relationship building still gets done in person.

Getting to sit down in person last night to break bread, catch up on life background and spar about ideas was 10x better than any zoom call could've been.

A big thanks to Tap and Barrel Founder Daniel Frankel and BC Business/Canada Wide Media CEO Ryan Benn for hosting us and sharing a bit more about your founder journeys. If you didn't know:

- Daniel originally started in media + film before pivoting to the restaurant world. He jumped into Tap and Barrell in 2012 and in just over 10 years has scaled his team to 1,300 staff across his locations 

- Ryan got his first phone call at 26 that he'd be taking over a $15m company with 70 staff and has been a builder, investor and operator ever since. His current day to day is now focusing on growing the Canada Wide Media brand which BC Business is a part of.  

My favourite takeaway from Daniel and Ryan's chat was reminding all of us that entrepreneurship is often a lonely journey. But if you're willing to prioritize time to surround yourself with other founders that inspire and hold you accountable, you're way more likely to enjoy the ride.

I couldn't agree more. Which makes me think we're gonna need to setup more dinners like these for young founders.
